lead: React is a JavaScript library for building a web page as a tree of small functions called components. Each component returns JSX, a syntax that looks like HTML. React turns that JSX into real DOM elements. The library exists because hand-written DOM updates become hard to track when many parts of a page depend on the same data. You describe the screen for the current data, and React does the DOM work. React is used in dashboards, e-commerce sites, UPI payment pages and admin consoles.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 (HTML elements and attributes) and Unit 3 (ES6 functions, arrow functions and modules).

sections.h3: The problem and the entry point

blocks.text: In Unit 3, a page changes through DOM methods. After a cart item is removed, you update the count span, the total div and the checkout button yourself. Every new feature must remember every affected node. One missed node leaves stale text on screen. React flips that responsibility: when data changes, React calls the component function again and updates the DOM from the new result.

items: CDN setup: load React, ReactDOM and Babel with script tags. Babel compiles JSX inside the browser.
Vite or create-react-app: a bundler compiles JSX before the browser runs it. npm create vite@latest starts a Vite project.
ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")) creates a React root on that element.
root.render(<App />) mounts the App tree: React builds elements and inserts the first DOM output under the root.

blocks.text: The one-line entry is ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(<App />). Mount means the first render of a React tree into a DOM node. Later data changes re-render affected components; props and state cover that.
JSX looks like HTML but is not HTML. A browser cannot run it. Babel, or a bundler such as Vite, transforms each JSX element into a function call before the code runs.

items: Return one parent element, or an empty fragment <>...</>, around siblings.
Curly braces hold a JavaScript expression: {title}. They cannot hold a statement such as if.
Use className for HTML class, and htmlFor for HTML for.
Close every tag. Self-closing tags end with a slash: <img />.
A capital first letter means a component, as in <Greeting />. A lowercase first letter means an HTML tag, as in <div>.

blocks.where: type is an HTML tag name as a string or a component function; props is an object of attributes or null; children are strings or nested React.createElement results.

blocks.text: For example, <h2>{title}</h2> becomes React.createElement("h2", null, title) when title is a variable. The classic transform is what exams ask for; newer React versions may use an automatic JSX runtime, but the element tree is the same.

A function component is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns JSX. function Header() { return <h1>Shop</h1>; } is a component. React calls it like any function and uses the returned element.

A class component extends React.Component and has a render() method: class Header extends React.Component { render() { return <h1>Shop</h1>; } }. Some syllabi call these React Classes. Function components are the default in new code.

Compose components by nesting them. App can return <div><Header /><PostList /><Footer /></div>. React calls App, then each child component. The result is a component tree. A stateless component has no state; it only uses props, covered in Chapter 5.2.

sections.h3: Styling and the ES6 pieces you reuse

items: External CSS: import a .css file once and apply classes with className.
Inline style: use a JavaScript object with camelCase keys, as in style={{color: "teal", fontSize: "16px"}}. The outer braces are JSX; the inner braces are the object.
CSS modules: import styles from "./Card.module.css", then className={styles.card}; class names are scoped to that file.
styled-components writes CSS inside JavaScript; Reactstrap gives Bootstrap 4 components such as <Button color="primary">.

blocks.text: Five ES6 features carry most React code. let and const give block scope. Arrow functions shorten callbacks and keep this from the enclosing scope. Destructuring pulls values out of props or objects. Spread copies arrays or objects into a new one. Modules split components across files with import and export. Unit 3 treats each fully.

figure.caption: The page is a tree: App renders Header, PostList and Footer; PostList renders three Post components. The browser DOM contains only their output, not the component names.

spec.aria: A component tree with App at the root, Header, PostList and Footer below it, and PostList holding Post 1, Post 2 and Post 3.

examples.question: A JSX snippet is <div className="card"><h2>{title}</h2><p>2 items</p></div> with title = "Dosa". (a) Write the equivalent React.createElement calls. (b) Write the HTML the browser finally shows. (c) State how many elements, how many createElement calls, and how many JavaScript expressions are evaluated.
steps: Read the outer element: type div, one prop className with value card, two children.
Convert the first child: <h2>{title}</h2> becomes React.createElement("h2", null, "Dosa"), because title evaluates to Dosa.
Convert the second child: <p>2 items</p> becomes React.createElement("p", null, "2 items").
Join them: React.createElement("div", {className: "card"}, React.createElement("h2", null, "Dosa"), React.createElement("p", null, "2 items")).
The DOM gets real elements; JSX className becomes the DOM attribute class. HTML: <div class="card"><h2>Dosa</h2><p>2 items</p></div>.
Count: three elements (div, h2, p), three createElement calls, and one JavaScript expression ({title}).
examples.answer:
The JSX becomes three React.createElement calls, the browser shows

Dosa

2 items

, and the counts are 3 elements, 3 createElement calls and 1 expression.
examples.check:
import re jsx = '

{title}

2 items

' elements = len(re.findall(r'<(div|h2|p)\b', jsx)) expressions = jsx.count('{') calls = elements print(elements) print(calls) print(expressions)

traps: JSX is not HTML: class becomes className, and for becomes htmlFor.
Two sibling elements need one parent or a fragment. return (<h1>A</h1><p>B</p>); is invalid.
<Greeting /> calls your component. <greeting /> is an unknown HTML tag because the first letter is lowercase.
Inline style uses an object, not a CSS string: style={{color: "teal"}}. Keys are camelCase, so fontSize, not font-size.
Curly braces in JSX hold an expression, not a statement. {if (x) ...} is invalid.

quiz.a: It creates a React root on the #root element and mounts the App tree inside it.

quiz.q: Which JSX attribute replaces HTML class, and which replaces for?
Why is <Greeting /> treated as a component but <greeting /> as an HTML tag?
quiz.a: JSX uses the case of the first letter: a capital starts a component reference, while lowercase is a tag name.

quiz.q: What job does Babel or the bundler do for JSX?
quiz.a: It transforms JSX into React.createElement calls before the browser runs the code.

quiz.q: A component returns <Header /><PostList /> with no wrapper. Explain the error and give one fix.
quiz.a: JSX must return one element, so two siblings are two children of the component call. Wrap them in a <div> or a fragment <>...</>.

beyond: Not for the exam. React now has Server Components and Suspense, which let parts of the tree render on the server and stream to the browser. Next.js and Remix build full-stack apps on these ideas. Signals and fine-grained reactivity appear in newer frameworks. Search for React Server Components, Suspense, Next.js App Router and signals.
